title: SHE WAS GIVEN LAND… BUT SHE REFUSED TO LIVE WITHOUT WATER: THE FORGOTTEN WOMAN WHO DARED TO ASK FOR MORE
paragraphs: SHE WAS GIVEN LAND… BUT SHE REFUSED TO LIVE WITHOUT WATER: THE FORGOTTEN WOMAN WHO DARED TO ASK FOR MORE

Her name was Achsah. Her inheritance was real. Her land was dry. And one courageous request revealed a truth about faith, provision, and the Father’s generosity that many believers desperately need to rediscover.
She had already received something valuable.
Land. An inheritance. A future.
From the outside, it might have looked like she had every reason to be satisfied.
But there was a problem.
The land needed water.
And Achsah understood something that many people discover only after years of struggling:
You can possess something valuable and still lack what is necessary to make it fruitful.
You can have a house and still long for peace.
You can have a marriage and still ache for tenderness.
You can have a ministry and still feel spiritually exhausted.
You can know the right Bible verses and still find yourself crying in the dark, wondering why your heart feels so empty.
And sometimes, the most dangerous thing a believer can do is pretend that needing help means lacking faith.
Achsah did not pretend.
She did not quietly accept the situation as though asking for provision would make her ungrateful.
She went to her father.
And she asked for springs.
What happened next was recorded in just a few verses of Scripture, yet the implications reach far beyond a small piece of land in ancient Judah.
Because buried inside this often-overlooked account is a question that may expose something about your own relationship with God.
Have you been trying to survive on dry ground while refusing to bring your needs before the Father?
Before we answer that, we need to meet the woman behind the story.
And we need to understand what the Bible actually says.
Achsah appears in Joshua 15:16–19, with a parallel account in Judges 1:12–15.
She was the daughter of Caleb, one of the most remarkable men in Israel's wilderness generation.
Caleb was not remembered because he never faced frightening circumstances.
He was remembered because he trusted the Lord when others allowed fear to overpower faith.
When twelve spies were sent to examine Canaan, ten returned with reports that discouraged the people.
The land was good, but its inhabitants seemed too powerful.
The obstacles appeared too great.
Caleb and Joshua, however, believed that Israel should obey God and trust His promise.
Numbers 14:24 records God's declaration that Caleb had followed Him wholeheartedly.
That faithfulness did not mean Caleb received his inheritance immediately.
He waited through decades of wilderness wandering.
He endured the consequences of an unbelieving generation.
And when the time came to claim his inheritance, Caleb was still ready to move forward.
In Joshua 14:12, he famously requested the hill country where formidable enemies remained.
He was not asking for an easy life.
He was trusting the God who had promised to be with him.
And somewhere within that family story stands Achsah.
A daughter raised in the shadow of extraordinary faith.
But here is what makes her account so compelling.
She would not merely be remembered as Caleb's daughter. She would demonstrate a remarkable willingness to ask for what was needed.
Joshua 15:16–17 tells us that Caleb offered his daughter Achsah in marriage to the man who captured Kiriath-sepher, also called Debir.
Othniel, the son of Kenaz, captured the city and became her husband.
We should not pretend that the marriage arrangements of ancient Israel were identical to modern expectations.
Achsah's story belongs to an ancient patriarchal society in which fathers exercised substantial authority over marriage arrangements.
The biblical account does not give us enough information to reconstruct every private feeling Achsah experienced about her marriage.
But it does preserve her initiative in a matter concerning her future.
And that initiative is significant.
The King James Version of Joshua 15:18–19 reads:
"And it came to pass, as she came unto him, that she moved him to ask of her father a field: and she lighted off her ass; and Caleb said unto her, What wouldest thou?
And she answered, Give me a blessing; for thou hast given me a south land; give me also springs of water. And he gave her the upper springs, and the nether springs."
Read those final words again.
He gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.
Not because the text says she manipulated him.
Not because she demanded something that belonged to someone else.
Not because she rejected the inheritance she had received.
She recognized a genuine need, made a specific request, and received a generous answer.
The Hebrew makes this moment even more beautiful when we examine it carefully.
Achsah says:
תְּנָה־לִּי בְרָכָה
Tenah-li verakhah.
Literally, "Give me a blessing."
The Hebrew word בְּרָכָה (berakhah) means "blessing" and, in this context, refers to a tangible benefit or gift.
Achsah was not requesting a vague emotional experience.
She was asking for something concrete.
Then she explained why.
כִּי אֶרֶץ הַנֶּגֶב נְתַתָּנִי
Ki erets ha-negev netattani.
The sense is, "For you have given me land in the Negev," or "land of the south."
The Hebrew נֶגֶב (negev) can refer to the southern region and carries associations with dry country.
The verse identifies the land's geographical character, while her request for water makes its practical significance unmistakable.
Then comes the request:
וְנָתַתָּה לִי גֻּלֹּת מָיִם
Ve-natattah li gullot mayim.
"And give me springs of water."
The expression גֻּלֹּת מָיִם (gullot mayim) refers to springs or water sources.
These were not decorative additions to her property.
In an agricultural society, reliable water could mean the difference between land that merely existed and land capable of sustaining people, animals, and crops.
Achsah was thinking about more than what she had received.
She was thinking about what would be necessary to live there.
And then Scripture says Caleb gave her:
גֻּלֹּת עִלִּיּוֹת וְאֶת־גֻּלֹּת תַּחְתִּיּוֹת
Gullot illiyyot ve'et gullot tahtiyyot.
The upper springs and the lower springs.
Notice something important.
The text does not say Achsah asked for a specific number of springs.
It tells us she asked for water sources, and Caleb granted both the upper and lower springs.
The narrative emphasizes the provision she received.
And the story ends there.
No extended speech.
No dramatic celebration.
No detailed account of how the land developed afterward.
Just a daughter who asked and a father who gave.
Yet sometimes Scripture leaves us with a scene so simple that we nearly miss its power.
Because the question is no longer merely what Achsah received.
The question becomes what her example can teach us without forcing the passage to say more than it actually says.
And this is where we must be careful.
Achsah's request was made to her earthly father, Caleb.
Joshua 15 is primarily an account of Judah's territorial inheritance, not a direct promise that every Christian who asks God for material abundance will receive it.
Caleb is not presented as a perfect representation of God the Father.
The upper and lower springs are not secret biblical codes for wealth, healing, or guaranteed success.
The passage does not teach that every hardship will disappear when we pray with enough confidence.
To claim otherwise would be to place promises into God's mouth that He has not made.
But the account does reveal a woman who recognized her need and was willing to ask for provision.
And when we bring that observation into conversation with the wider teaching of Scripture, we discover something deeply encouraging.
Jesus Himself taught His followers to approach their heavenly Father in prayer.
In Matthew 7:7–11, He invited them to ask, seek, and knock.
Then He asked what father would give his child a stone when the child requested bread.
His conclusion was breathtaking.
If imperfect human parents know how to give good gifts to their children, how much more will the heavenly Father give good things to those who ask Him?
Jesus was not teaching that prayer gives us control over God.
He was revealing the goodness of the Father.
And this matters because some of us have learned to associate asking with disappointment.
Perhaps you grew up in a home where expressing a need made you feel like a burden.
Perhaps you were told to be grateful and stop complaining, even when something genuinely important was missing.
Perhaps you asked someone for help once, only to have your vulnerability used against you.
So you learned to stay quiet.
You became independent.
You became capable.
You became the person everyone else depended on.
And somewhere along the way, you began treating your relationship with God the same way.
You pray for everybody else.
You encourage everybody else.
You remind others that God is faithful.
But when the house is quiet and the responsibilities finally stop, you are left carrying needs you barely know how to name.
You are exhausted.
And you are afraid to admit it.
Because you think a stronger Christian would not feel this way.
But listen carefully.
The presence of a need is not proof of the absence of faith.
Sometimes faith is demonstrated precisely when we acknowledge that we cannot sustain ourselves.
Achsah had land.
She needed water.
And she asked.
What have you been afraid to ask God about?
Not because He is unaware of it.
Matthew 6:8 reminds us that the Father knows what His children need before they ask.
But because prayer is not simply the transfer of information.
It is an expression of dependence, trust, worship, and relationship.
Maybe your need is not financial.
Maybe your greatest struggle is the bitterness you have carried for years.
You smile when people mention forgiveness.
You know what the Bible says.
But deep inside, you are still replaying what happened.
Still remembering the betrayal.
Still wondering why the person who hurt you seems to have moved on while you remain trapped in the consequences.
Or perhaps your marriage has become a place where two people share responsibilities but rarely share their hearts.
The bills are paid.
The children are cared for.
The photographs still look beautiful.
But something precious has become painfully distant.
Or perhaps the dry ground is inside you.
You still attend church.
You still know the worship songs.
You still say "Amen."
But the Scriptures you once read with hunger now sit unopened for days.
You have become skilled at looking spiritually healthy while quietly struggling to believe that God still welcomes you.
And the enemy would love for you to confuse your exhaustion with God's rejection.
But that is not the Gospel.
The Gospel does not begin with humanity proving that it has enough strength.
It begins with the reality that we are sinners who cannot rescue ourselves.
Romans 3:23 declares that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory.
Our deepest problem is not simply that life feels dry.
It is that sin has separated humanity from the holy God who made us.
And no amount of determination, religious performance, money, or personal improvement can erase our guilt.
We need mercy.
We need forgiveness.
We need reconciliation.
We need a Savior.

And this is where the story of Achsah becomes a doorway into a greater biblical truth—not because Achsah secretly symbolizes Jesus, but because the whole testimony of Scripture ultimately leads us to understand our need for Him.
Achsah asked her father for water to sustain her inheritance.
But Jesus Christ came to accomplish something infinitely greater.
He came to save sinners and give eternal life.
Consider another encounter involving a woman and water.
In John 4, Jesus met a Samaritan woman at Jacob's well.
She came seeking ordinary water.
Jesus began speaking to her about living water.
He said in John 4:14:
"But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life."
That conversation was not about agricultural irrigation.
It was about the life that Jesus gives.
The Samaritan woman had a complicated personal history, and Jesus knew the truth about her life.
Yet He did not walk away from her.
He spoke to her.
He exposed what needed to be brought into the light.
And He revealed Himself as the Messiah.
Imagine that.
A woman came to a well carrying a waterpot.
She encountered the One who could give her something no earthly well could supply.
John 4:28 tells us that she left her waterpot and went into the city.
The object she had brought to the well suddenly became secondary to the Person she had encountered there.
And here is the connection we must never confuse.
Achsah needed physical water, and her father supplied it.
The Samaritan woman needed the spiritual life Christ alone could give.
Both accounts involve women and water, but they are distinct events with different purposes.
Their connection is illustrative, not a claim that Joshua 15 directly predicts John 4.
Yet together they can remind us of a truth we desperately need.
Some needs can be met through earthly provision. But the deepest thirst of the human soul can be satisfied only through Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is where this article finds you.
You have been asking God to change your circumstances.
But have you also asked Him to change your heart?
You have been praying for relief.
But have you brought your sin into the light?
You have been asking Him to restore what you lost.
But have you surrendered the parts of your life you keep trying to control?
Because the greatest gift God gives us is not a comfortable life.
It is Himself, through His Son.
And we cannot speak of that gift without speaking of the cross.
Jesus did not come merely to inspire struggling people.
He came to redeem sinners.
He lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He bore our sins in His body on the tree, as 1 Peter 2:24 declares.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again, according to the Scriptures.
The cross exposes the seriousness of our sin.
The resurrection announces the victory of our Savior.
And the grace of God calls us not merely to admire Jesus, but to repent and believe in Him.
This is why the Gospel is more than motivational language.
It is not a promise that every earthly dream will come true.
It is the announcement that guilty people can be forgiven, the spiritually dead can be made alive, and those who were far from God can be brought near through the blood of Christ.
That is grace.
Not a reward for pretending we have everything together.
Not a prize for the most impressive religious performance.
Grace is God's undeserved favor, given through Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that unmistakably clear.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works, so that no one can boast.
And Ephesians 2:10 continues by showing that those saved by grace are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Do you see the order?
We do not obey in order to purchase salvation.
We obey because God's grace has begun transforming us.
We do not give money to make God love us.
We give generously because He has already loved us in Christ.
We do not serve to earn a place in His family.
We serve because we belong to Him.
And that distinction matters more than any fundraising appeal ever could.
Your offering cannot buy forgiveness.
And a struggling believer who cannot afford to give is not less precious to Jesus than someone who can.
The widow who gave two small coins in Mark 12:41–44 reminds us that God sees the heart behind the gift.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not come from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Christian generosity is meant to flow from love, not fear.
And when believers freely support sound biblical ministry, they can participate in making the Gospel known and helping others grow in Christ.
That is a beautiful privilege.
Not a spiritual purchase.
A response of gratitude.
But before we speak about supporting Gospel work, there is something more personal we need to confront.
What if the greatest obstacle in your spiritual life right now is not that God has refused to listen?
What if you have stopped coming honestly before Him?
You have learned how to pray respectable prayers.
Safe prayers.
Prayers that sound mature in public.
But there are things you have not said aloud to God in a long time.
"Lord, I am angry."
"Lord, I am jealous."
"Lord, I am tired of pretending."
"Lord, I keep returning to the same sin."
"Lord, I believe You are good, but I am struggling to trust You."
"Lord, I need help."
And perhaps those last four words are the hardest.
I need help.
Because somewhere inside, you have convinced yourself that needing help is humiliating.
But the Scriptures repeatedly show God's people crying out to Him in distress.
David did it.
Hannah did it.
Jeremiah did it.
The psalmists did it.
And in the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus Himself prayed to the Father in the anguish of His approaching suffering.
Hebrews 4:15–16 tells us that our great High Priest is able to sympathize with our weaknesses, having been tempted as we are, yet without sin.
Then comes the invitation:
"Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need."
Not the throne of humiliation.
Not the throne of rejection.
The throne of grace.
And the word translated "boldly" comes from the Greek παρρησία (parrēsia), conveying confidence or freedom of speech.
It does not mean arrogance.
It means that through Christ, believers may approach God with confidence rather than terror.
That confidence is not rooted in our perfection.
It is rooted in Jesus, our High Priest.
Achsah could approach Caleb because he was her father.
But the Christian's confidence before God rests on something even greater: the finished work of Jesus Christ, through whom believers have access to the Father.
And that should change how we pray.
Not by making us demanding.
But by making us honest.
Not by persuading us that God owes us everything we desire.
But by reminding us that He welcomes His children to bring their needs before Him.
Sometimes His answer is yes.
Sometimes His answer is wait.
Sometimes His answer is no.
And sometimes His grace sustains us through a hardship He has not yet removed.
Paul knew this.
In 2 Corinthians 12:7–10, he pleaded with the Lord three times concerning his thorn in the flesh.
The Lord did not remove it.
Instead, He answered:
"My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness."
That is an important balance to Achsah's story.
Caleb gave the springs Achsah requested.
But Christians must not assume that every request will be answered in the same way.
God's generosity is real.
His wisdom is perfect.
And His faithfulness does not depend on whether our circumstances become easy.
Sometimes He provides the water.
Sometimes He gives endurance in the wilderness.
And sometimes He teaches us that His presence is more precious than the outcome we were begging to receive.
But in every circumstance, the believer's hope remains anchored in Christ.
Not in a guaranteed earthly result.
In a faithful Savior.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because many of us are willing to ask God for blessings while resisting the repentance He commands.
We want peace without surrender.
Forgiveness without confession.
Restoration without truth.
Spiritual strength without abiding in Christ.
We want God to water the land while we refuse to uproot the sin that is choking our lives.
But Jesus loves us too much to leave us comfortably enslaved to what is destroying us.
He calls us to repent.
To turn away from sin.
To trust Him.
To follow Him.
Not because His grace is insufficient, but because genuine grace changes the direction of a person's life.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions.
Grace does not merely comfort us in our brokenness.
It teaches us to walk in newness of life.
And that is where the Gospel Warrior message becomes deeply personal.
Not because scandal is harmless.
Not because consequences disappear.
Not because repentance erases every wound we have caused.
But because Jesus Christ can redeem people whose stories have been marked by shame, rebellion, failure, and sin.
Think about Peter.
He promised loyalty to Jesus.
Then denied Him three times.
Imagine the shame of hearing the rooster crow.
Imagine remembering the words of the Lord.
Imagine realizing that the very loyalty you boasted about had collapsed under pressure.
But Peter's failure was not the final chapter of his story.
The risen Jesus restored him in John 21 and entrusted him with the responsibility to care for His sheep.
Peter was not restored because his denial had been insignificant.
He was restored by the mercy of the Savior he had denied.
And that is the kind of grace we preach.
Grace that does not lie about sin.
Grace that does not minimize wounds.
Grace that does not call darkness light.
Grace that leads sinners to repentance and points them to the One who forgives.
Maybe you have your own Peter moment.
A decision you regret.
A relationship you damaged.
A season when you knew what was right and deliberately chose what was wrong.
Perhaps people still remember the worst version of you.
Perhaps you remember it too.
And every time you try to move forward, shame whispers that your past is your permanent identity.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, your past is not greater than His redeeming power.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares that anyone in Christ is a new creation.
That does not mean the past never happened.
It means that union with Christ brings a new identity and a new life.
Repentance is not pretending that the damage was imaginary.
It is turning toward the Savior who can forgive, transform, and teach us to walk differently.
And sometimes restoration also requires confession, restitution where possible, accountability, and patient rebuilding of trust.
Grace is not permission to escape responsibility.
It is power to begin living truthfully.
So what does all of this have to do with Achsah?
More than we might first imagine.
She teaches us, through a brief historical example, that recognizing a need and speaking honestly about it need not be shameful.
She reminds us that provision matters.
That wisdom considers what is necessary for the future.
That gratitude and asking are not always opposites.
And the wider Scriptures remind us that our ultimate dependence belongs to God.
But the story also confronts another question.
Are you asking only for what will make your life easier, or are you asking God to make your life fruitful for His glory?
There is a difference.
One prayer says, "Lord, give me more so I can feel secure."
Another says, "Lord, provide what I need, and teach me to use what You entrust to me faithfully."
One seeks gifts while ignoring the Giver.
The other seeks the Giver and receives His gifts with thanksgiving.
Jesus said in John 15:5:
"I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing."
Without Him.
Those three words should stop us.
Because we can build impressive things without spiritual fruit.
We can gather attention without making disciples.
We can become successful in the eyes of the world while becoming increasingly distant from the heart of Christ.
We can even speak about God publicly while neglecting Him privately.
And perhaps that is the most frightening kind of dryness.
Not the dryness everyone can see.
The dryness hidden beneath religious activity.
The kind that allows a person to keep performing while their soul is starving for honest fellowship with God.
If that describes you, do not turn this moment into another promise to try harder without Christ.
Come to Him.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Turn from what needs to be abandoned.
Receive His mercy.
Open His Word again.
Pray honestly.
Seek the fellowship and accountability of faithful believers.
And remember that spiritual growth is not measured by how emotional you feel during a single article.
It is seen over time in a life increasingly shaped by the truth and love of Jesus Christ.
There is one more detail about Achsah that deserves attention.
Her story is not recorded only once.
It appears in Joshua 15 and again in Judges 1.
The repetition places her request within the account of Israel's settlement in the land.
We should not invent a hidden reason for why the narrative appears twice.
But its preservation means that generations of Scripture readers have been able to encounter this brief account of a woman who took initiative regarding her inheritance.
Her words are few.
Her request is specific.
And her story remains.
Perhaps that is another lesson worth remembering.
A life does not have to be loud to matter.
A person does not need a long biography in Scripture to offer a meaningful example.
Faithfulness is not always accompanied by applause.
Sometimes it looks like recognizing a responsibility.
Sometimes it looks like asking a necessary question.
Sometimes it looks like refusing to pretend that everything is fine.
And sometimes it looks like quietly trusting God with the next step.
If you have made it this far, I want to ask you something.
Not as a test.
Not as a performance.
But as an invitation to spiritual honesty.
Where is the dry ground in your life?
Is it your prayer life?
Your marriage?
Your relationship with your children?
Your battle with temptation?
Your inability to forgive?
Your exhaustion from caring for everyone while neglecting your own need for rest and spiritual nourishment?
Or is it the hidden fear that, after everything you have done, Jesus could never truly welcome you?
Whatever it is, do not let shame convince you to remain silent before God.
He already knows the truth.
And if you are in Christ, you do not have to approach Him as someone trying to earn permission to be loved.
You come through the Savior who died and rose again.
If you have not yet trusted Christ, the invitation is not to purchase a blessing or perform enough good deeds to become acceptable.
It is to repent and believe the Gospel.
Jesus Christ is the Savior of sinners.
And His mercy is greater than the false hope that we can save ourselves.
Maybe today your most important prayer will not be eloquent.
Maybe it will be whispered through tears.
"Lord Jesus, forgive me."
"Lord, teach me to trust You."
"Father, I need Your help."
And perhaps, for the first time in a long time, you will stop pretending.
You can write "Lord, I need Your grace" if that is your prayer today.
Or "Pray for me" if you are walking through a difficult season and would value encouragement from other believers.
If God has already carried you through a season of spiritual dryness, consider sharing a little of your testimony. Your experience may encourage someone who currently feels alone.
You do not need to reveal private details or painful experiences you are not ready to share.
Honesty before God matters more than public disclosure.
Not because every post must go viral.
But because someone in your circle may need a reminder that the Gospel is for weary sinners, not merely people who appear to have their lives together.
Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, those who have drifted from faith, and even those who are still exploring Christianity to walk with us through God's Word.
Because the mission is not simply to produce content people admire.
It is to help people encounter biblical truth, grow in their understanding of the Gospel, and follow Jesus more faithfully.
That is also why I want to share something about the work behind Gospel Warrior.
These resources are intended to encourage Bible reading, strengthen discipleship, and help believers continue learning beyond a single article.
And we want to keep building.
We want to continue making Scripture-centered resources available.
We want to reach people who may never enter a church building but might pause long enough to read a message about Jesus on their phones.
We want to encourage the exhausted believer, challenge the complacent Christian, welcome the searching soul, and point the repentant sinner toward the hope of the cross.
That work takes time, effort, and resources.

It should not be treated as a replacement for whatever biblical giving responsibilities you understand yourself to have toward your local church, nor should it be considered a payment for spiritual favor.
Your local church, your family responsibilities, and your financial circumstances matter.
Please do not give under pressure or beyond what you can responsibly afford.
It helps make the work more sustainable.
Those products are simply an added expression of appreciation.
The greater purpose is to support a continuing work of biblical encouragement, discipleship, and Gospel proclamation.
Read.
Learn.
Pray.
Share the free resources.
Encourage someone else.
Help a friend find a message that points to Christ.
Your presence is not measured by a monthly payment.
Your value before God cannot be bought.
And the Gospel we proclaim remains the Gospel of grace.
One thoughtful share may open a conversation.
One personal tag may encourage a struggling friend.
One sincere comment may remind another believer that they are not alone in the fight of faith.
One testimony may direct someone's attention away from despair and toward the mercy of Jesus.
And one act of generosity, freely offered, may help sustain resources that continue serving others.
We cannot know how far every act of faithfulness will reach.
But we can be faithful with what God has placed in our hands.
And now, before you leave, return with me to the scene where this story began.
A woman.
An inheritance.
A dry landscape.
A father listening to his daughter's request.
Achsah asked for springs of water.
And Caleb gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.
The Bible does not tell us what Achsah said afterward.
It does not describe her emotional reaction.
It does not record a long speech about gratitude.
It simply tells us what she asked and what she received.
And perhaps that simplicity is enough.
Because you do not need to embellish Scripture to be moved by it.
You only need to listen carefully.
Achsah recognized what she needed for the land entrusted to her.
And she spoke.
Today, you may be standing in a very different kind of place.
Perhaps your life has been scarred by choices you wish you could undo.
Perhaps you have experienced rejection that made asking for help feel dangerous.
Perhaps you have been faithful through a long season that has produced more tears than visible answers.
Or perhaps your circumstances are outwardly comfortable, but you know your heart has drifted far from God.
Wherever this finds you, remember what the Gospel announces.
Jesus Christ did not come to save people who could prove they had no need.
He came to seek and save the lost.
He did not die for imaginary sinners.
He died for real sinners with real guilt.
And He did not remain in the grave.
He rose again.
So bring your need to Him.
Bring your confession.
Bring your doubts.
Bring your weariness.
Bring your gratitude.
Bring your willingness to obey even when the answer is difficult.
And trust Him with the outcome.
Because the greatest hope of the Christian life is not that every dry season will end tomorrow.
It is that nothing can separate those who belong to Christ from the love of God in Him, as Romans 8:38–39 declares.
The Father who has given His Son has not abandoned His children.
And the Savior who conquered the grave is worthy of our trust even when the road ahead remains hard.
Achsah's story begins with land and ends with springs.
But the Christian's hope begins and ends with Jesus.
You may still be standing on dry ground, but in Christ, your deepest hope is not buried beneath it.
